analysis.one_liner: Gives makers of new antibiotics a sellable extra year of monopoly on another drug, to spur antibiotic development.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by a Republican with two Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2018, and died there without ever receiving a markup or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would award drug companies that develop antibiotics for dangerous drug-resistant bacteria a 12-month extension of market exclusivity. That extension would not have to be used on the antibiotic itself — the company could sell or transfer it to delay generic competition on a different, often far more profitable, drug. The bill caps the program at ten awards, requires a 5% contribution from each sale toward research on resistant pathogens, and directs the FDA to maintain a priority list of drug-resistant bacteria.
analysis.who_benefits: Drug companies that develop antibiotics for drug-resistant bacteria, and the brand-name drug makers who could buy the transferred exclusivity to keep cheaper generics off the market longer on other drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Antibiotic developers and brand-name drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Awarding a 12-month exclusivity extension for drugs designated as priority antimicrobial products is intended to make developing new antibiotics financially worthwhile, since such drugs are used sparingly and are otherwise unprofitable.
The exclusivity can be sold or transferred to other brand drugs, so a small antibiotic developer could monetize it even if the antibiotic itself sells poorly.
Each time exclusivity is transferred, the seller must contribute 5% of the sale value to the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health for early-stage research on drug-resistant pathogens.

Companies receiving the designation must track resistance data, adopt stewardship guidelines, make the drug available to susceptibility-test device makers early in development, and submit periodic stewardship assessments.

The FDA would establish a committee and a public list of critical drug-resistant bacterial and fungal priorities to steer designations, and GAO and CDC would later study whether the program worked and what it cost federal spending.

analysis.who_pays: Patients, insurers, and Medicare and Medicaid, because the transferred exclusivity delays generic competition on other brand drugs, keeping their prices higher for up to an additional year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients and payers buying delayed-generic drugs

drawbacks.text: The mechanism works by extending monopoly protection on other drugs, which delays cheaper generic versions and raises drug costs for patients, insurers, and government health programs.

The value of the exclusivity can be sold to whichever drug best monetizes it, so the subsidy may flow to blockbusters rather than to the most medically needed products; the bill's own answer is a GAO study of these impacts only years later.

There is no guarantee the incentive produces new antibiotics: the program is capped at ten awards, and the required study of whether any new drug was actually developed does not begin until at least five years after enactment.
The 5% contribution to NIH research is small relative to the market value of an extra year of exclusivity on a major drug, so most of the subsidy stays with the industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targets is real: drug-resistant infections are a growing threat and new antibiotics are commercially unattractive to develop. But the payment mechanism — letting companies buy an extra year without generic competition on unrelated drugs — pushes the cost onto patients and payers through higher drug prices, and the public benefit is uncertain because it depends on antibiotics actually being developed later. A more direct approach, such as public funding for antibiotic development, would have put the cost on taxpayers rather than on drug purchasers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2018 and sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 28, 2018 by Rep. John Shimkus, joined by Rep. Cardenas.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
It received no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Generic drug makers and the patients and payers who buy their drugs were spared the delayed competition the bill would have created, but patients facing drug-resistant infections gained nothing because the hoped-for antibiotic incentive never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Generic drug makers and patients buying generics

for.name: Rep. John Shimkus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Rep. Tony Cardenas
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction as the bill's Democratic cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill with two Democratic cosponsors, and no one is recorded opposing it — it simply died without action, so there was never a vote to reveal a party split.

industries.note: Antibiotic developers would receive a free 12-month exclusivity extension they could sell, and other brand-name makers could buy it to delay generics on their own blockbusters. Because the industry's gain comes directly from keeping cheaper generic competition off the market longer, its interest runs against patients' and payers' interests on drug prices.
Each transferred exclusivity extension delays or prevents generic approval on a targeted brand drug for up to an additional year, costing the generics industry sales.

industries.industry: Health insurers and public health programs (Medicare, Medicaid)
industries.note: Longer brand-drug monopolies mean paying brand prices longer, raising costs for insurers, Medicare, and Medicaid.
As a condition of designation, antibiotic sponsors must make their products available to these device makers early in development, giving the device industry earlier access.

industries.industry: Biomedical research (NIH Foundation-funded early-stage antibiotic research)
industries.note: Five percent of the value of every exclusivity sale must go to NIH-foundation research on drug-resistant pathogens.
